source_title: Above-normal maximum temperatures likely over most parts of India in November: IMD
source_excerpt: New Delhi Above-normal maximum temperatures are likely over most parts of India in November, except for some regions along the foothills of the Himalayas where normal to below-normal maximum temperatures are expected, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Saturday (October 31, 2026) in its monthly forecast. It also stated that during the month, above-normal minimum temperatures are expected over most parts of the country, except in many parts of central and eastern India where normal to below-normal minimum temperatures are likely. Bay of Bengal weather system set to revive rain in Keralam from November 1 Bay of Bengal weather system set to revive rain in Keralam from November 1 According to IMD, a low-pressure area formed over South Andaman Sea and adjoining areas of Andaman and Nicobar Islands is likely to intensify into a depression over southeast Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas of Andaman Sea and Andaman and Nicobar Islands on Sunday Bay of Bengal weather system set to revive rain in Keralam from November 1 storyline 1 The IMD noted that in November, below-normal rainfall is likely over most parts of the country except for some areas in central, northwest, and Northeast India, where normal to above-normal rainfall is likely. India as a whole is likely to witness 77% of Long Period Average (LPA) rainfall during the month. LPA refers to the rainfall recorded over a particular region for a given interval, such as a month or season, averaged over a long period, typically 30 to 50 years. The LPA of rainfall over the country during the month of November, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is about 29.7 mm. The LPA of rainfall over the region during November, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is around 118.7 mm, according to the IMD. The Department highlighted that, currently, very strong El Nino conditions are prevailing over the Equatorial Pacific Ocean. The latest Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecast System (MMCFS) and other global climate model forecasts indicate that very strong El Nino conditions are likely during November-December. El Nino is one of the three phases of the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate phenomenon characterised by changes in sea temperatures along the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, accompanied by fluctuations in the atmosphere overhead. ENSO also has a neutral phase. A very strong El Nino disrupts normal temperature and rainfall patterns across many regions. It can also bring severe drought to some regions, heavy rainfall and flooding to others, and increased heat across large parts of the world.
